paragraphs.heading: What they are
paragraphs.text: Ripple marks are sedimentary structures that indicate sediment was agitated by water, as a current or as waves, or directly by wind. Current ripple marks, also called unidirectional or asymmetrical ripple marks, have a lopsided profile. The slope facing up-current is gentle and the slope facing down-current is steeper. The down-current slope sits at the angle of repose, and that angle depends on the shape of the sediment.

paragraphs.heading: Reading the flow
paragraphs.text: The side of a ripple with the gentle slope is called the stoss, and the steeper side is called the lee. The current always runs up the stoss side and then down the lee side. This can be used to work out how the current was flowing at the time the ripple formed.

paragraphs.heading: Ripples made by waves
paragraphs.text: Wave-formed ripples develop where surface waves set the water moving back and forth, and that motion shifts sediment across the bed. They commonly have roughly symmetrical profiles, with crests that are straight or gently winding. Symmetry is not a sure test, however. Wave-formed ripples are not the only symmetrical ones, and waves that are shoaling or breaking may move the water unequally in opposite directions, which results in asymmetric wave ripples. Wave-formed ripples are most often preserved in sediment laid down in shallow seas, lakes and tidal flats.

paragraphs.heading: Ripples made by wind
paragraphs.text: Aeolian ripples are small bedforms produced when wind moves loose sediment by processes called saltation and surface creep. Their crests lie roughly across the direction in which the sediment is moving overall. The most common small ones are impact ripples, which develop as saltating grains interact with grains resting on or moving along the surface. Repeated impacts tend to move grains from the troughs toward the crests, and this makes the ripple pattern migrate downwind. Where the sediment has grains of different sizes, the coarser grains may become concentrated near the crests.

paragraphs.heading: Megaripples
paragraphs.text: Aeolian megaripples are larger bedforms, sitting between ordinary impact ripples and dunes in scale. On Earth their wavelengths run from several tens of centimetres to several metres. They typically develop in sediment that is poorly sorted or bimodal, where finer saltating grains make coarser grains move by shorter hops or by surface creep. The coarser grains may form an armoured layer, especially near the crests.

paragraphs.heading: Ripples preserved in layers
paragraphs.text: When sediment is deposited while current or wave ripples are migrating, ripple cross-laminae form. Migrating ripples laid over one another produce a series of these cross-laminae. Ripple cross-laminae always have a steeper dip downstream.
